title: What to Do Before Applying for a Mortgage
meta_description: General guidance on preparing to apply for a mortgage before you start touring homes, from FN Home Group's Faith Nance.
summary: A few simple steps before you apply can make the mortgage process smoother and help you understand your options.
body:
Before you start touring homes, it's worth taking a little time to prepare for the mortgage application process. While every lender and every borrower's situation is different, there are a few general steps that tend to help.

Review your credit report

Many buyers request a copy of their credit report before applying so there are no surprises. If you notice anything that looks incorrect, you can look into how to dispute it directly with the credit bureaus.

Gather your documentation

Lenders typically ask for recent pay stubs, tax returns, bank statements, and identification. Having these ready ahead of time can help the process move more smoothly once you're ready to apply.

Think about your budget, not just your approval amount

A lender can tell you how much you're approved to borrow, but that number isn't always the same as what feels comfortable for your monthly budget. It's worth thinking through your full financial picture, not just the maximum loan amount.

Talk to more than one lender

Comparing loan programs, rates, and closing costs from a couple of different lenders can help you understand your options. Faith is happy to share names of lenders she's worked with, but you're always welcome to work with any lender you choose.

Ask questions early

If anything about the process feels unclear, ask before you're under a contract deadline. A good lender should be willing to explain things in plain language.

title: What First-Time Buyers Should Expect
meta_description: A friendly overview of what to expect as a first-time homebuyer in Southern Middle Tennessee, from Faith Nance of FN Home Group.
summary: Buying your first home involves a lot of new terminology and steps. Here's a plain-language overview of what the experience tends to look like.
body:
If you're buying your first home, it's completely normal to have a lot of questions. Here is a general overview of what the experience tends to involve, so you know roughly what's ahead.

Getting a sense of your budget

Many buyers start by speaking with a lender to understand what they may be able to borrow and what a monthly payment could look like. This step often happens before you start seriously touring homes.

Working with a buyer's agent

A buyer's agent represents your interests throughout the process, from touring homes to negotiating an offer. Faith takes time to explain buyer representation clearly so you understand what she does on your behalf.

Touring homes and narrowing your search

This is often the most enjoyable part, and also the part where your priorities may shift as you see more homes. It's normal for your must-have list to change along the way.

Making an offer

Once you find a home you love, your agent helps you put together an offer based on the home's condition, comparable sales, and your goals.

Inspections and next steps

After your offer is accepted, most buyers schedule a home inspection to better understand the property's condition before moving forward.

It's okay to ask "why"

Every step of this process has a purpose, and Faith would rather over-explain than leave you guessing. If something doesn't make sense, ask.

title: How a Comparative Market Analysis Works
meta_description: Learn what a Comparative Market Analysis (CMA) is and how it helps sellers understand pricing, from Faith Nance of FN Home Group.
summary: A CMA is one of the tools Faith uses to help sellers understand where their home may fit in today's market.
body:
If you're thinking about selling, you've probably heard the term Comparative Market Analysis, or CMA. Here's a general explanation of what it is and how it's used.

What a CMA looks at

A CMA generally compares your home to similar properties that have recently sold, are currently under contract, or are currently listed for sale in your area. It typically considers factors like square footage, bedroom and bathroom count, lot size, condition, updates, and location.

Why it's not the same as an online estimate

Automated home value tools use public data and algorithms, but they can't walk through your home, see recent updates, or account for local nuances the way a hands-on review can. A CMA involves a more personalized look at your specific property and current market activity.

How Faith uses a CMA

Faith uses a CMA as a starting point for a conversation about pricing strategy, not as a single fixed number. Pricing a home involves weighing market conditions, your timeline, and your goals together.

It's a living document

Market conditions can shift, so a CMA prepared today may look different in a few months. If you're not ready to sell yet, Faith is happy to revisit your home's position in the market when the time is right.

title: What Happens After an Offer Is Accepted
meta_description: A general overview of the steps that typically follow an accepted offer, from Faith Nance of FN Home Group.
summary: Getting your offer accepted is exciting, but there are still several steps ahead before closing day.
body:
Congratulations, your offer has been accepted! Here's a general look at what tends to happen next, though the exact steps and timeline can vary by transaction and contract terms.

Earnest money

Buyers typically submit earnest money shortly after the contract is signed. This deposit is generally held in escrow and applied toward your purchase at closing, subject to the terms of your contract.

Inspections

Most buyers schedule a general home inspection, and sometimes additional specialized inspections, within a set window defined in the contract.

Negotiating repairs

Depending on what the inspection finds, buyers and sellers may negotiate repairs, credits, or simply proceed as-is. This is a normal part of many transactions.

Appraisal

If you're financing your purchase, your lender will typically order an appraisal to confirm the home's value supports the loan amount.

Final loan approval

Your lender will continue processing your loan file, which may include additional documentation requests as you approach closing.

Final walkthrough and closing

Most buyers complete a final walkthrough shortly before closing to confirm the home's condition, followed by signing closing documents and receiving the keys.

title: Preparing Your Home for Listing Photos
meta_description: Practical, general tips for preparing your home before professional listing photos, from Faith Nance of FN Home Group.
summary: A little preparation before photo day can help your home's online listing make a strong first impression.
body:
Most buyers see your home online before they ever step inside, so listing photos matter. Here are some general tips to consider before photo day.

Declutter and depersonalize

Clearing countertops, tidying closets, and putting away personal items can help buyers picture themselves in the space.

Deep clean

A thorough cleaning, including windows, floors, and often-missed spots like baseboards, can make a noticeable difference in photos.

Maximize natural light

Open blinds and curtains, turn on lights, and consider the time of day photos are taken.

Tend to curb appeal

Mow the lawn, tidy landscaping, and consider a clean front entry, since exterior photos are often the first thing buyers see.

Put pets and pet items away

Litter boxes, food bowls, and pet beds are usually best tucked away for photos.

Talk to Faith about staging

Depending on your home, Faith may suggest light staging adjustments to help highlight your home's best features.

title: Understanding Earnest Money
meta_description: A plain-language explanation of earnest money and how it generally works in a real estate transaction.
summary: Earnest money is one of the more commonly misunderstood parts of a real estate contract. Here's a general explanation.
body:
Earnest money often causes confusion for buyers, so here's a general, plain-language explanation.

What it is

Earnest money is a deposit a buyer typically submits shortly after a purchase agreement is signed, showing they're serious about moving forward with the purchase.

Where it goes

Earnest money is generally held by a neutral third party, such as a title company or escrow agent, rather than going directly to the seller.

How it's applied

At closing, earnest money is typically credited toward the buyer's down payment or closing costs, subject to the terms of the contract.

What can happen to it

Depending on the contract terms and contingencies, earnest money may be refundable or non-refundable in certain circumstances. Because this varies by contract, it's important to read your agreement carefully and ask questions before signing.

This article is general information only. For specific questions about how earnest money applies to your contract, Faith recommends reviewing your agreement closely and consulting a real estate attorney if needed.

title: Inspection vs. Appraisal: What's the Difference?
meta_description: Understand the general difference between a home inspection and a home appraisal, explained by Faith Nance of FN Home Group.
summary: These two terms are often confused, but they serve very different purposes in a real estate transaction.
body:
Buyers often ask about the difference between an inspection and an appraisal. While both typically happen after an offer is accepted, they serve different purposes.

Home inspection

A home inspection is generally arranged by the buyer and focuses on the physical condition of the home, looking for issues with systems like the roof, HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and structure. The inspector typically provides a detailed report of findings.

Home appraisal

An appraisal is usually ordered by the lender (when financing is involved) and focuses on determining the home's market value to confirm it supports the loan amount. An appraiser typically compares the home to similar recently sold properties.

Why both matter

An inspection helps a buyer understand what they're purchasing, while an appraisal helps confirm the home's value for lending purposes. They can lead to different types of conversations and, occasionally, renegotiations during a transaction.

title: Questions to Ask Before Selling
meta_description: Helpful questions to consider before listing your home, shared by Faith Nance of FN Home Group.
summary: Selling a home is a big decision. These questions can help you think through your goals before you list.
body:
Before you list your home, it can help to think through a few questions. There's no single right answer, but working through these can help clarify your plan.

What is your timeline?

Are you hoping to sell quickly, or do you have flexibility? Your timeline can influence pricing strategy and how you approach preparation.

Where are you moving next?

Do you need to buy another home at the same time, relocate, or downsize? Coordinating a sale and a purchase can add complexity worth planning for early.

What condition is your home in?

Are there repairs or updates worth making before listing, or would it make more sense to sell as-is? This is worth discussing honestly with your agent.

What's motivating the sale?

Understanding your "why" can help guide decisions about pricing, timing, and negotiation flexibility.

What questions do you have about the process?

There's no such thing as a silly question. Faith would rather you ask upfront than feel unsure later.

title: A Moving Checklist for Middle Tennessee
meta_description: A general moving checklist to help you plan a smoother move within or into Middle Tennessee, from Faith Nance of FN Home Group.
summary: A general checklist to help keep your move organized, whether you're relocating across town or across the country.
body:
Moving involves a lot of moving parts (no pun intended). Here's a general checklist to help you stay organized.

4-6 weeks before

Research moving companies or rental trucks, begin decluttering, and start collecting moving supplies.

2-4 weeks before

Schedule utility transfers or new service setup at your new home, submit a change of address, and begin using up food and cleaning supplies you don't want to move.

1-2 weeks before

Confirm moving day logistics, pack non-essential rooms, and label boxes by room.

Moving week

Pack an essentials box with items you'll need immediately, confirm final walkthrough details if you're closing on a sale, and double-check utility start dates at your new home.

After the move

Update your address with your bank, employer, and other accounts, register vehicles if you've moved across county or state lines, and take time to explore your new community.

Faith's Client Resource Center includes downloadable checklist placeholders that go into more detail for buyers and sellers.

title: When You're Interested in Moving but Not Ready Yet
meta_description: Not ready to buy or sell yet? Here's how to start preparing thoughtfully, from Faith Nance of FN Home Group.
summary: You don't have to be ready to move tomorrow to start asking questions today. Here's how to think about the in-between stage.
body:
Not every conversation about real estate needs to end in a transaction right away. If you're thinking about a move someday but you're not ready yet, that's a completely normal place to be.

It's okay to just be curious

Maybe you're wondering what your home might be worth, curious about a neighborhood, or simply trying to understand the process before you're ready to act. Faith welcomes these conversations without pressure.

Use the time to prepare

If you know a move is somewhere in your future, you might use this time to research neighborhoods, understand financing options, or simply keep an eye on your home's value over time.

Stay informed, not overwhelmed

Faith's Resource Hub is designed so you can learn at your own pace, whether that's browsing a few articles now or requesting a full consultation later.

Reach out whenever you're ready

There's no expiration date on asking questions. When the time feels right, Faith is happy to help, whether that's next month or next year.
